Rajat Rao

Geospatial Analyst | Environment Consultant

Exploring social and environmental complexities, one spatial curiosity at a time.

docs.title: About
docs.text:
I am a geospatial analyst with a keen interest in understanding the complex relationships between people, places, and the environment. In my previous work, I managed large geospatial datasets and conducted critical analyses of India's high-altitude ecosystems. I use GIS, remote sensing, Python, and R to explore environmental patterns, investigate geographical questions, and uncover stories hidden within spatial data. I am particularly drawn to understanding landscapes, river systems, terrain, and glaciers. For me, every map is an opportunity to ask questions about a place and encourage space-based thinking in people, which I believe is an essential first step in resolving any issue.

A short film I made based on my M. Sc. thesis. It spatially maps 20 years of rampant development along the IT belt in Bengaluru.

docs.title: Mammal Distributions in the High Altitudes of Jammu & Kashmir
docs.text:
R SSDM Google Earth Engine QGIS Camera trapping Species distribution modelling

  • Context: Research collaboration between NCF and the Department of Wildlife Protection, J&K
  • Duration: ~2 years
  • Study area: High-elevation regions of Jammu & Kashmir (Kishtwar Himalayas)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This project started as an assessment of snow leopard range in the high altitudes of Jammu & Kashmir. Partway through, we widened the scope to the other mammals recorded on the same camera traps. The result is a set of distribution models for ten species, several of which had not been modelled in this region before.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
• Occurrence records: Camera trap detections from stations deployed over 1.5-2 years across different seasons. Species were identified manually from the images to build the training dataset.
  • Climate covariates: The 19 WorldClim bioclimatic variables (BIO1-BIO19).
  • Terrain and vegetation covariates: Ruggedness, slope and NDVI, derived in Google Earth Engine.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
1. Covariate preparation. Terrain and NDVI layers were generated in Google Earth Engine and combined with the bioclimatic layers. Collinearity among the 22 variables was assessed with the usdm package.
  2. Modelling. I used the SSDM package in R to build stacked species distribution models. Eight algorithms were compared for each species: GAM, MaxEnt, GBM, GLM, CTA, ANN, RF and MARS.
  3. Validation. Model performance was evaluated with TSS and Kappa, and the best-performing models were retained.
  4. Mapping. Final outputs were laid out and published as maps in QGIS.

docs.title: Species modelled
docs.text: Species Scientific name Brown bear Ursus arctos Himalayan ibex Capra sibirica Long-tailed marmot Marmota caudata Mountain weasel Mustela altaica Musk deer Moschus leucogaster Red fox Vulpes vulpes Snow leopard Panthera uncia Eurasian stoat Mustela erminea Stone marten Martes foina Yellow-throated marten Martes flavigula

docs.title: Key Findings
docs.text: The models gave distribution maps for all ten species, several of them for the first time in this region. Each species showed a distinct pattern tied to terrain and landscape type, with different parts of the landscape acting as niches for different species.

docs.title: Predicted distributions
docs.text: Snow leopardHimalayan ibexBrown bearRed foxStone martenMusk deerStoat

docs.title: Results
docs.text: The models gave distribution maps for all ten species, several of them for the first time in this region. Each species showed a distinct pattern tied to terrain and landscape type, with different parts of the landscape acting as niches for different species.

docs.title: Limitations and lessons
docs.text:
• Small mammals were excluded. We initially tried to include pikas and other small mammals, but they could not be reliably told apart in camera trap images because of their size.
  • Image processing was the main bottleneck. Identifying species across lakhs of images to build the training dataset took a large share of the project time. A better workflow for screening and labelling images would have saved a lot of effort.

docs.title: Lahaul Wildlife Management Plan
docs.text:
• Role: Spatial analysis and maps
  • Tools: QGIS, Google Earth Engine
  • Effort: About two weeks, as one contributor to a larger plan
  • Status: Submitted to the Himachal Pradesh Forest Department

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Lahaul Forest Division in Lahaul and Spiti sits between the Pir Panjal and the Trans-Himalaya. It supports snow leopard, Himalayan brown bear, ibex, musk deer and Himalayan tahr, and is also a working agro-pastoral landscape. The management plan sets out how the Forest Department can conserve wildlife and habitat, reduce human-wildlife conflict and curb poaching across the division.

I was one of several contributors. My part was spatial: I made three of the plan's maps and wrote the text around the hydropower map.

docs.title: What the plan covers
docs.text:
• Wildlife and habitat: mammals, birds and medicinal plants of the valley, and snow leopard status from the state-wide PAWS survey.
  • Human-wildlife conflict: livestock and crop depredation, free-ranging dogs, garbage, and a prevent-offset-inform framework for human-bear conflict.
  • Pressures on habitat: grazing, disease transmission, medicinal plant harvest and poaching.
  • Management actions: village-level micro-plans, compensation, conservation education, research and monitoring, and staff training.
  • Infrastructure: the effect of linear infrastructure and proposed hydropower projects on the landscape.

docs.title: My contribution
docs.text:
I produced the following maps in QGIS and Google Earth Engine. The RAI analysis was done in R.

Camera TrapsSnow Leopard DistributionHydro ProjectsRelative Abundance Index

docs.title: Hydropower and development
docs.text: The plan ends with the infrastructure section. Many development projects are proposed across the valley, including hydropower, so the plan argues that wildlife spaces need a management plan in place before those projects proceed. It also notes the climate and disaster risks to hydropower, such as changing rainfall, discharge uncertainty and siltation. Local concerns about land and livelihoods are noted too. The Hydro Projects map shows where the proposed projects fall in the valley. It draws on Chandel & Rana (2024), Current World Environment, 18(3), 1345–1355.

docs.title: Data and tools
docs.text:
• QGIS for cartography and spatial layers
  • Google Earth Engine for terrain and river layers
  • R for RAI analysis

The plan was submitted to the Forest Department and is not publicly available.
